article.title: America’s Wealth Inequality Crisis: Why Tax Cuts Won’t Fix the Economy
article.author: Charles D. Hayes
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. We have a monumental math problem in America, and what is broken cannot be repaired by tinkering around the edges. The Jurassic Republicans were right about one thing: There is no free lunch. But they were mistaken in believing there is such a thing as a truly free market. Every economic transaction depends on infrastructure, education, public safety, environmental protection, and countless other necessities that markets cannot simply conjure out of thin air. Yet the prices we pay for goods and services seldom reflect their full costs to society. The Hidden Costs of the “Free Market” Environmental degradation, pollution, public health consequences, and the depletion of natural resources are often excluded from the price tag, leaving society and future generations to pay for damages that private transactions fail to account for. Economists call these negative externalities , but in plain English, they amount to shifting costs onto people who had no say in creating them. Someone pays for all of it. The question is who. Beginning roughly half a century ago, the political influence of concentrated wealth helped transform taxation into something to be feared rather than understood as the price of maintaining civilization. The wealthy became indispensable job creators, progressive taxation became an assault on success, and government became the enemy. National Debt and the Cost of Neglect The results deserve examination. We have accumulated a national debt exceeding $40 trillion, with annual interest costs around a trillion dollars. The condition of our airports, roads, bridges, and electrical infrastructure on the world stage is a global embarrassment. Wars, recessions, emergencies, spending decisions, and tax reductions all contributed. But repeatedly reducing revenue without corresponding reductions in obligations has undeniably compounded the problem. For decades, politicians have promised Americans the benefits of civilization without adequately paying for them. Now the bill is coming due. A country cannot indefinitely finance its obligations through borrowing while allowing an ever-growing concentration of wealth to escape proportionate taxation. Nor can it sustain a prosperous middle class while permitting the rewards of economic growth to flow disproportionately toward those already wealthy. RAND’s $79 Trillion Finding: What the Bottom 90 Percent Lost $79 trillion. That’s the additional income a 2025 RAND Corporation working paper estimates the bottom 90 percent of American earners would have received between 1975 and 2023 had they continued to receive their 1975 share of income. That cumulative figure is expressed in inflation-adjusted 2023 dollars. For 2023 alone, the estimated shortfall was $3.9 trillion. After sleeping on this revelation, it occurs to me that if the annual shortfall remained at that level for the next three years, the cumulative total would reach nearly $91 trillion by the end of 2026, still measured in 2023 dollars. We cannot tax-cut our way out of this predicament. We cannot deregulate our way out of it. And we certainly cannot trickle down our way out of it. The arithmetic is merciless. We must raise sufficient revenue to meet our obligations, and that means restoring meaningful progressive taxation, particularly on the enormous incomes and accumulated wealth at the top. Right-wing capitalists can huff and puff like the Big Bad Wolf, threatening to blow down the Three Little Pigs’ house of straw, but no amount of bluster about trickle-down economics is going to solve our problems. What is truly amazing, though, is how many times we have fallen for the same empty promises, despite decades of evidence that the promised prosperity has failed to trickle down to those who need it most. Restoring Progressive Taxation to Rebuild the Middle Class A recent study by the RAND Corporation estimates that the bottom 90 percent of American income earners would have received an additional $79 trillion between 1975 and 2023 had they continued to receive the same share of national income they received in 1975. To my mind, that represents an extraordinary transfer of income into the upper echelons of American society. Calling efforts to reverse that trend “socialism” does nothing to explain or justify what happened. The real irony is that we watched this enormous redistribution of wealth unfold in slow motion, scarcely recognizing what was happening until the damage had already been done. Now we are staring at a national debt of $40 trillion, and I repeat, ad nauseam , that the only way to right the ship of state is to restore progressive tax rates similar to those that helped create and sustain the American middle class in the first place. There is no ideological escape from mathematics. No magic formulas. A civilization that refuses to pay for its own maintenance is ultimately choosing its own deterioration. And no amount of political rhetoric can repeal the fundamental reality that what we refuse to invest in today will become a far greater burden on the generations who follow.
